stem: A 60-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests show elevated bilirubin and cholestatic liver enzymes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot's triad) with cholestatic LFTs = acute (ascending) cholangitis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows a dilated gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid, and she has a positive Murphy’s sign. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: Acute calculous cholecystitis → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission (within ~72 h–1 week) — fewer readmissions, same complication rate. A related 438 recall noted the early window.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with right lower quadrant pain at McBurney’s point. The pregnancy test is negative. The physician is unsure if the presentation is classical for appendicitis. What is the most appropriate next step?
expl: When the presentation isn't classical in an adult (and pregnancy is excluded), CT confirms appendicitis and excludes other causes — the doctor: "CT is the standard in adults nowadays".

why.B: Operating without confirmation when the picture is unclear risks a negative appendectomy.
why.C: Skipping imaging is acceptable only in pregnancy/when imaging is inconclusive and suspicion stays high.
why.D: Antibiotics before a diagnosis is made is wrong.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with fever, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. CT scan reveals a 5-cm pericolic abscess adjacent to the sigmoid colon. He is hemodynamically stable and has no signs of generalized peritonitis. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: Diverticulitis with a large (> 3–4 cm) pericolic abscess in a stable patient without generalized peritonitis (Hinchey Ib) → IV antibiotics + CT-guided percutaneous drainage; elective resection may follow.

why.A: Antibiotics alone work for small abscesses (< 3 cm); 5 cm needs drainage.
why.B: Emergency resection is for generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III–IV) or failed drainage.
why.D: An abscess is never observed without treatment.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents 5 days after onset of vomiting and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. CT scan shows a 3-cm peri-appendiceal abscess. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Interval appendectomy after initial conservative treatment

expl: A peri-appendiceal abscess presenting late (5 days) → IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage; operating on the inflamed mass is difficult and risks more complications.

why.A: Immediate appendectomy in a walled-off abscess risks bowel injury/ileocaecal resection.
why.B: Observation alone doesn't treat an abscess.
why.D: Interval appendectomy is optional later — the immediate step is drainage + antibiotics.

stem: A 75-year-old male presents with abdominal distension and constipation. Abdominal X-ray shows a coffee-bean shaped loop of colon in the left lower quadrant. The patient is hemodynamically stable with no signs of peritonitis. What is the best initial management?
expl: Sigmoid volvulus ("coffee-bean" loop in the LLQ) in a stable patient without peritonitis → endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) decompression/detorsion with a rectal tube, then elective sigmoidectomy.

why.A: Emergency colectomy is for peritonitis, ischaemia or failed decompression.
why.D: Caecostomy has no role in sigmoid volvulus.

stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting. Imaging shows an appendiceal abscess measuring 3 cm. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.t: IV antibiotics with percutaneous drainage of the abscess

expl: A 3-cm appendiceal abscess in a stable patient → IV antibiotics with percutaneous drainage.

why.A: Immediate surgery in a walled-off abscess is more hazardous.
why.D: Delayed laparoscopic appendectomy without drainage leaves the abscess.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with severe abdominal pain, guarding, rigidity, and signs of sepsis. He is hemodynamically unstable. What is the next step?
expl: Generalized peritonitis (guarding, rigidity) with sepsis in an unstable patient → resuscitate and take him to emergency laparotomy (source control). Unstable patients don't go to CT.

why.A: CT in an unstable patient is dangerous.

stem: A 52-year-old man underwent an appendectomy for acute appendicitis. Histopathology revealed an incidental appendiceal adenocarcinoma <1.5 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.t: Appendiceal stump re-excision with wider margins only

expl: Appendiceal adenocarcinoma (unlike a small carcinoid) is treated like colon cancer — right hemicolectomy for oncological clearance (nodes).

why.A: Chemotherapy alone isn't the treatment of a resectable primary.
why.D: Stump re-excision doesn't remove the lymph nodes.

stem: What is the most common site of diverticulitis?
expl: In Western/Middle-Eastern populations diverticulitis is most common in the sigmoid colon (highest intraluminal pressure). Right-sided diverticula are more common in Asian populations.

why.A: Ascending colon is uncommon (except in Asians).

stem: A 45-year-old patient undergoes an appendectomy for suspected acute appendicitis. Pathology reveals a carcinoid tumor of the appendix, <2 cm in size, confined to the appendix with clear margins. What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: No further surgery; appendectomy is sufficient

expl: Appendiceal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) < 2 cm, confined, with clear margins → appendectomy alone is curative. Right hemicolectomy is for > 2 cm, mesoappendix/base involvement, nodes, or high grade.

stem: A 95-year-old with poor ASA and multiple comorbidities has gallbladder stones and signs of cholecystitis but a normal CBD. What is the management?
ansText: Percutaneous cholecystostomy tube — drains the infected gallbladder under local anaesthesia in a patient too unfit for cholecystectomy.

stem: An 80-year-old thin man with no previous surgery has large-bowel obstruction, and no hernia is found. What is the most likely cause (not the most common)?
ansText: Neoplasm — colorectal cancer is the most likely cause of LBO in an elderly patient with a virgin abdomen and no hernia (then volvulus, diverticular stricture).

stem: A patient with symptoms of appendicitis is found to have an abscess. What is the best management?
ansText: Percutaneous drainage and antibiotics (± interval appendectomy later).

stem: A 95-year-old patient with a poor ASA score and multiple comorbidities presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and signs of acute cholecystitis. Imaging confirms gallbladder stones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid with a normal common bile duct (CBD). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?( same idea)
expl: Acute cholecystitis in a 95-year-old with a poor ASA and multiple comorbidities → percutaneous cholecystostomy (source control under local) ± antibiotics; cholecystectomy later if fit.

why.E: May fail; drainage is needed with pericholecystic fluid.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with mild acute pancreatitis. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: TPN, IV fluids, pain control, antibiotics
Enteral feeding, IV fluids, pain control Questions about gallbladder a lot of as lap chole, cholangitis,percutaneous, also about percutaneous fistula

expl: Mild AP → IV fluids (LR), analgesia and early enteral (oral) feeding. TPN and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.

why.A: TPN and antibiotics are not indicated.

stem: What is the most common cancer found in the appendix?
ansText: Carcinoid / neuroendocrine tumour — the commonest appendiceal neoplasm (usually incidental at the tip); appendectomy cures most < 2 cm.

stem: A patient with diverticulitis presents with a pericolic abscess and signs of localized peritonitis. According to the Hinchey classification, what is the stage? -

opts.t: Hinchey Class Ia (Pericolic or mesenteric abscess) -

expl: Hinchey: 0 = mild clinical diverticulitis; I = pericolic/mesocolic abscess (modified: Ia confined pericolic inflammation/phlegmon, Ib pericolic abscess); II = pelvic/distant abscess; III = purulent peritonitis; IV = faecal peritonitis. The keyed option's description ("pericolic or mesenteric abscess") is Hinchey I — the "Ia" label is the source's.

why.A: Correct (source key — Hinchey I, pericolic abscess).
why.C: The label "Ib" fits a pericolic abscess in the modified scale, but the option describes a "confined abscess" vaguely; the source key is A.

stem: A CT scan reveals diverticula in the ileum of a patient. Which of the following is true about diverticula? -

opts.t: Diverticula are composed of all layers of the bowel wall. -
Diverticula are only found in the colon.

srcNote: No answer key is stated in this source version.
expl: The source had no key. Multiple diverticula in the small bowel/colon are acquired "false" (pulsion) diverticula — mucosa and submucosa herniating at weak points where vessels enter. (Meckel's diverticulum is the exception: congenital, true, single.)

why.C: Acquired diverticula are false (no muscle layer); only true diverticula like Meckel's contain all layers.
why.D: They occur in the oesophagus, duodenum, jejunum and ileum too.

stem: A VITALLY STABLE patient presents with Cecal Volvulus, What’s the most appropriate mx ?
srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. B (Acute abdomen) (Bowel obstruction)
expl: The source key for this recall was B. Caecal volvulus is treated surgically — right hemicolectomy (or caecopexy). Endoscopic detorsion succeeds rarely (~30%) and is not standard, unlike sigmoid volvulus.

why.A: Works for sigmoid, rarely for caecal volvulus.
why.C: Colonoscopy doesn't fix a caecal volvulus.

stem: 40 year old female presented with signs and symptoms of bowel obstruction,past surgical history hysterectomy 5 years ago ,what's the most likely cause of her condition?
expl: Any previous abdominal/pelvic operation (hysterectomy) → adhesions are the commonest cause of SBO.

why.A: Possible, but adhesions are commonest after surgery.
why.D: Cancer is less likely at 40 after surgery.

stem: 45 year old female presented with severe epigastric pain in the hypochondrium, mild icterus, febrile, leukocytosis. What's the best next step to confirm diagnosis
expl: Fever, leukocytosis, upper abdominal pain and mild icterus → biliary pathology (cholecystitis/cholangitis) → ultrasound is the first and best test.

stem: Old age (~70 yo) with chronic mild pain and constipation, now presents with sudden Left Lower abdominal pain with distention, N&V & absolute constipation. X-ray showed. Diagnosis? Original source figure: 439 B Q4
expl: Elderly with chronic constipation, sudden LLQ pain, gross distension and absolute constipation, with the X-ray (bent inner tube/coffee bean) → sigmoid volvulus.

why.B: Toxic megacolon follows severe colitis with bloody diarrhoea, not chronic constipation.

stem: Recall — the diagnosis shown (image/case) was:
ansText: Bowel ischaemia (the recall gave only the answer).

stem: 33-year-old women presented to the ER complaining of right upper quadrant pain associated with fever, nausea and vomiting. Physical examination revealed marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant area of the abdomen. BP (115/56), HR (83), Temp (38.2), RR (17), WBC (16.5, N=4-10.5), US: thick wall of the gallbladder, pericholecystic fluid and multiple gallstones but the CBD were not dilated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: No answer key stated in this source version.
expl: The source had no key. Acute calculous cholecystitis (fever, leukocytosis, thick wall, pericholecystic fluid, stones) with a normal CBD in a young fit woman → admit for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission.

why.B: Cholecystostomy is for patients too unfit for surgery.
why.C: Delayed surgery is old practice; early surgery is safer and shortens stay.
why.D: ERCP is only needed for CBD stones; the CBD is normal.

stem: Rovsing sign is associated with which of the following conditions?
expl: Rovsing's sign — pressing the LIF causes pain in the RIF — is a sign of appendicitis.

why.B: Pancreatitis signs are Cullen's and Grey Turner's.

stem: 25-year-Old healthy man with no previous history of abdominal surgery. presented to the emergency department complaining of severe colicky abdominal pain for 6 hours associated with frequent vomiting, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal distention with exaggerated bowel sounds. Which of the following Is the most appropriate initial step in management?
expl: SBO in a patient with no previous surgery (virgin abdomen) → the first thing is to examine the groins for an obstructed hernia — the commonest cause in this setting.

why.C: Surgery comes after finding the cause/resuscitation.
why.D: CT comes after a careful examination.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is known to have multiple small gallstones, presented to the ER complaining of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting for 18 hours. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness. Blood pressure 120/65 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Temperature 37.8 Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result: (Normal value) WBC 13.4 (4-10.5 x 10 9 L) Serum amylase 5.4 (0.54-2.02 nkat/L) Alkaline phosphatase 3.2 (0.7-1.9 ukat/L) Total bilirubin 34 (3.5-16.5 umol/L) Direct bilirubin 19 (1.5-6.5 umol/L) Which of the following is the appropriate initial management?
srcNote: ? (Gallstone related disorders, Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Source key C (marked "?"). Gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis (stable, no fever, mild cholestasis) → initial management is IV crystalloid resuscitation; ERCP only if cholangitis/persistent obstruction; US to confirm the cause.

stem: An 18 year old man is brought to the emergency department because he has had continuous pain in the lower quadrant for the past 18 hours. On examination, the abdomen is soft but tender to palpation with rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. No other abnormalities noted. BP: 100/60 mmHg HR: 80/min RR: 18/min Tem: 37.8 C SpO2: 100% on room air Which of the following is the best next step?
expl: An 18-year-old man with RLQ pain and rebound — CT abdomen and pelvis confirms appendicitis and excludes alternatives (the doctor's standard in adults).

why.C: Plain X-ray is not diagnostic for appendicitis.
why.D: Laparotomy is unnecessary — laparoscopic appendectomy after diagnosis.

stem: Female pt with a history of RUQ colicky pain for 5 days and slight fever, they gave her 1L of 0.9 NS but she did not improve. What is the most likely dx of the pt?
expl: RUQ colicky pain for days with fever not settling = acute cholecystitis (colic settles within hours; cholangitis needs jaundice).

stem: Pt presented to the ER with RLQ pain for 8 hours, Temp: 38C, the abdomen was soft and lax, what is the next appropriate management? (missed scenario but pt with appendicitis)
expl: Suspected appendicitis with a soft abdomen in an adult → CT to confirm.

stem: A patient presents with Cecal Volvulus, What’s the most appropriate mx
srcNote: (Acute abdomen?) (Bowel obstruction) Source note (438 B Q11): Answer: B (Acute abdomen?) (Bowel obstruction)
expl: Caecal volvulus → operative management: right hemicolectomy, or caecopexy in selected patients. Endoscopic detorsion rarely works.

stem: pt present with RUQ pain, fever, jaundice and pruritus, itching, dark urine , all lab results are high including liver enzymes and high GGT, imaging shows one stone in gallbladder, no increase gallbladder thickness, but CBD is dilated and biliary tree is dilated as well. What will the work up be for?
expl: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice (Charcot's triad) with a dilated CBD and cholestatic LFTs = acute cholangitis (infected obstructed bile duct). Gallbladder wall is normal.

why.A: "Obstructive jaundice" ignores the fever — infection makes it cholangitis.
why.D: Cholecystitis needs a thick inflamed gallbladder and doesn't cause jaundice.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presented to the ER complaining of right upper quadrant pain for 12 hours. Patient was nauseated and vomited twice. Physical examination revealed marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant area of the abdomen. Blood pressure 115/60 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Temperature 38 C, Respiratory rate 22 /min. Test results were Normal. US: multiple gallstones. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: Source key was BC; corrected — see explanation. (Gallstone related disorders)
expl: Acute cholecystitis (12 h of RUQ pain, fever, tachycardia, tenderness, gallstones) → early (urgent) cholecystectomy in the same admission — the doctor's teaching. The source accepted both B and C; waiting for symptoms to subside is old practice.

why.A: Elective surgery weeks later risks recurrent attacks.
why.B: Old "cool-down then operate" approach — not current practice.
why.D: Antibiotics and analgesia alone treat the attack but not the cause.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with fever, vomiting and significant right lower quadrant abdominal pain for 4 days. Her examination reveals rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. What is the next appropriate management?
expl: RLQ pain for 4 days with fever and rebound — late presentation; CT shows perforation/abscess and guides management (drainage vs surgery).

why.C: Laparotomy is too much without imaging.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a history of sudden lower abdominal pain for 12 hours, associated with progressive abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting and absolute constipation. Physical examination revealed grossly distended abdomen, generalized discomfort with normal bowel sounds with empty rectum. Erect abdominal X-RAY showed massively distended bowel loop pointing to the right upper quadrant with "coffee bean " sign. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly man, sudden lower abdominal pain, progressive gross distension, vomiting, absolute constipation (with the X-ray) → sigmoid volvulus.

why.A: Cancer gives a slower history of change in bowel habit.
why.B: Volvulus is a closed-loop obstruction, but the specific diagnosis is sigmoid volvulus.
why.D: Diverticulitis causes fever and LIF tenderness, not massive distension.

stem: A 75-year-old woman with history of congestive heart failure presents with diffuse abdominal pain for 2 hours. On examination, she has distended abdomen, diffuse severe tenderness, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Occult blood test was positive. Lab results are remarkable for High WBC and Lactic acid. Blood Pressure 95/60 mmHg, Heart Rate 110/min, Respiratory Rate 22/min, Temperature 38.5° C, Sp02 100% on Room air.
expl: Elderly with CHF (low flow/emboli), sudden diffuse pain, hyperactive bowel sounds and occult blood → acute mesenteric ischaemia.

why.A: Obstruction causes colic, vomiting and distension over longer — no occult blood.
why.D: Cholecystitis is RUQ and has no occult blood.

stem: A 57 year-old man presented to emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with fever, and yellowish discoloration of sclera for 5 days. On examination he was febrile (39.50C). and jaundiced with mild right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness. Laboratory values showed high white blood cell count (16x 109/L), and high LFTs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation
expl: RUQ pain, fever and jaundice (cholangitis) → the initial imaging is transabdominal US (stones, duct dilatation); ERCP follows for drainage.

why.B: ERCP is therapeutic after imaging and resuscitation.
why.D: MRCP is for when US is inconclusive.

stem: 62-year-old presents with vomiting, abdominal distention and constipation for the past 2 days. He was found to have large bowel obstruction. No past history of surgery. What is the most common etiology?
expl: In older adults with large-bowel obstruction and no previous surgery, malignancy (colorectal cancer) is the commonest cause.

why.C: Adhesions cause small- not large-bowel obstruction.
why.D: Hernias usually obstruct the small bowel.

stem: Elderly patient presented with a picture of acute abdomen, what is the investigation of choice?
expl: Keyed: in an elderly patient with an acute abdomen, start with a chest X-ray (erect) — free air, basal pneumonia, cardiac clues — before CT. The doctor: "always start with plain films".

why.A: Supine AXR complements it but misses free air.

stem: A 35 years old man came to ER with epigastric pain and vomiting for 5 days , HR=100 BP 100/65 elevated WBC and Amylase , what is the initial investigation of choice?
expl: In any pancreatitis-like scenario where perforation hasn't been excluded, the first investigation is an erect chest X-ray (air under the diaphragm). The source note: if no erect CXR was mentioned, it's the answer.

stem: A 38 year old woman presented to the emergency department with a history of epigastric abdominal pain for 5 days radiating to the back, associated with frequent vomiting. She is known to have multiple gallstones. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal distension and tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory values including complete blood count, liver function tests were all normal. Erect chest X-ray showed left pleural effusion Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
expl: After 5 days serum amylase may normalise but urinary amylase stays raised (~10 days) → urine amylase. CT is used when diagnosis is still uncertain.

stem: 33-year-old women presented to the ER complaining of right upper quadrant pain for 8 days associated with fever, nausea and vomiting. Physical examination revealed marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant area of the abdomen. Blood pressure 115/56 mmHg Heart rate 83 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 17/min Test Result Normal value WBC 16.5x109/L (4-10.5x109/L) US: thick wall of the gallbladder, pericholecystic fluid and multiple gallstones. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
expl: Source key B. Acute cholecystitis presenting late (8 days) is past the ideal early window — the classic answer is antibiotics now and delayed (interval) cholecystectomy. The doctor favours early surgery when presenting within the window.

why.A: Not a standard term (cholecystostomy is for unfit patients).

stem: An 80 years old man was presented to the ER department with a history of severe abdominal pain of 16 hours associated with diarrhea and vomiting. He is known case of atrial fibrillation and congestive heart failure presently on digoxin. On examination abdomen is distended with guarding and rectum is empty. WBC count 28*10 and abdominal plain x-ray shows edema of the bowel. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
srcNote: Source key was D; corrected — see explanation. Source note (433 A Q36 (p. 184)): Answer: A (Acute abdomen) Source answer keys differ; the original keys are preserved above.
expl: AF on digoxin + severe pain, distension, guarding, WBC 28 and bowel-wall oedema = acute mesenteric ischaemia with peritonitis (infarcted bowel) → surgical exploration (resect dead bowel ± embolectomy) after resuscitation and heparin. The sources keyed D and A differently; peritonism means the bowel is likely dead — surgery is needed.

why.A: Heparin is started in all, but with peritonism it doesn't replace laparotomy.
why.C: Embolization would worsen ischaemia (endovascular revascularization is different).
why.D: Antibiotics alone don't treat infarcted bowel.

stem: a 59-year-old woman who is known to have atrial fibrillation presented to the emergency complaining of sudden severe diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting. Physical examination revealed a non tender abdomen. Laboratory values showed white blood cell count: 27x10^9/mm^3 and serum amylase is 285 IU. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: AF + sudden severe diffuse pain with a non-tender abdomen (pain out of proportion) = acute mesenteric vascular occlusion (SMA embolus).

why.C: Pancreatitis gives epigastric tenderness, raised amylase.

stem: An 80-years old man. Known case of ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, and gallstones. Presents with a history of severe abdominal pain and vomiting for one day. On examination he looks sick, in pain, with blood pressure of 105/60. Heart rate of 110 beats/minute and temperature of 38.3 C. His abdomen is mildly rigid with no rebound tenderness.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly with IHD and AF, severe pain, sick and hypotensive → mesenteric ischaemia (embolus).

why.A: AAA would give a pulsatile mass and back pain.
why.C: Gallstones raise pancreatitis, but AF + sick + pain out of proportion → ischaemia.
why.D: Intestinal angina is chronic post-prandial pain with weight loss.

stem: similar image with a scenario what is the diagnosis “fever and shortness of breath”: Original source figure: 435 A Q29 (p. 135)
expl: The image shows free air under the diaphragm → perforated viscus — even if the story mentions fever and dyspnoea (a perforation causes sepsis and splinting).

why.C: Pneumonia gives consolidation, not subdiaphragmatic air.

stem: Pt. presented to the ER with abdominal pain for 12 h. Physical examination showed upper abdominal tenderness .serum amylase was 250 .erect x-ray was done what is the next most appropriate imaging
expl: Upper abdominal pain with amylase 250 (mildly raised) after an erect X-ray excluded perforation → US to look for gallstones (cause of pancreatitis) and the biliary tree.

why.B: CT is for diagnostic doubt or severity after 72 h.
why.C: Urine amylase helps in late presentations.

stem: Tip from the recalls — in an acute pancreatitis-like scenario, which investigation is the answer if it hasn't been done yet?
srcNote: Recall supplied without a complete set of labelled choices.
ansText: Erect chest X-ray — always exclude perforation (which can also raise amylase) before labelling pancreatitis.

stem: A 65-year-old man known to have cardiomyopathy, presented to the ER with a history of severe, sudden central abdominal pain for 8 hours associated with nausea and vomiting. He passed loose stools once. On examination, the abdomen was showing mild diffuse tenderness, with slightly exaggerated bowel sounds. Blood pressure 115/65 mmHg Heart rate 82 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 17/min Test Result (Normal value) WBC 26.7 (4-10.5 x 10 9 L) Serum amylase 2 (0.54-2.02 nkat/L) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Cardiomyopathy (embolic source), sudden severe central pain, vomiting, one loose stool, soft abdomen → mesenteric vascular occlusion.

why.B: Dissection gives tearing pain to the back with pulse deficits.
why.D: Pancreatitis gives epigastric tenderness and amylase rise.

stem: A 68-year-old man admitted through ER with a history of sudden severe lower abdominal pain associated with progressive abdominal distention and constipation for 24 hours. On examination the abdomen was hugely distended, tympanic with tenderness over the left iliac fossa. Digital rectal examination revealed empty rectum. Blood pressure 100/55 mmHg Heart rate 92 /min Temperature 38.5 Respiratory rate 21/min Test Result Normal value WBC 22 4-10.5 x 10 9 L Abdominal plain x-ray: Y-shaped shadow surrounded by a hugely distended colon arising from the periphery with ‘coffee bean’ sign. Which of the following is the appropriate intervention?
expl: Sigmoid volvulus (huge tympanic distension) in a stable patient → sigmoidoscopy with rectal (flatus) tube insertion for detorsion; elective sigmoidectomy later.

why.A: Primary anastomosis in an unprepared, distended colon is risky as first step.

stem: 25 yrs male obese with right lower quadrant pain and tenderness with nausea and anorexia with high WBC Count What is your next step in management?
expl: RLQ pain, anorexia, nausea, high WBC in an obese adult (exam unreliable) → CT.

why.A: Open surgery without imaging isn't needed.
why.B: US is poor in obese patients.
why.D: Diagnostic laparoscopy if imaging is inconclusive.

stem: A patient has signs and symptoms of perforation, and imaging already shows air under the diaphragm. What would you do next?
srcNote: ?? Missing choices you already know there is air under diaphragm through imaging why would you order erect x-ray again?
ansText: No further imaging (a repeat erect X-ray adds nothing) — resuscitate (ABC, NPO, IV fluids, NGT, Foley, antibiotics, PPI, analgesia) and proceed to urgent surgical repair (Graham omental patch). The source had no options or answer.

stem: patient 58 years old comes to the emergency complaining of nausea and vomiting with appendicular mass with no collections was treated conservatively and resolved what to do next?
expl: After an appendicular mass resolves conservatively in an older patient (> 40), colonoscopy is needed to exclude caecal cancer presenting as a mass.

why.A: Interval appendectomy is optional; it doesn't exclude cancer.
why.B: Interval appendectomy is optional; it doesn't exclude cancer.

stem: 48 year old man presented to the emergency department complaining of severe sudden epigastric pain for 6 hours. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, normal blood pressure with upper abdominal tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial imaging?
expl: Sudden severe epigastric pain = perforation until proven otherwise → erect CXR for free air.

stem: A 45 year old obese woman who is known to have cholelithiasis, presents to the emergency room complaining of severe continuous mid-abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting for 16 hours. On examination, she has a low-grade fever with epigastric tenderness. Laboratory values showed: WBC count: 12.000 (4.000-10.000/ml) and serum amylase 2000 mmol/1 (23-125). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Known gallstones + continuous epigastric/mid-abdominal pain with vomiting = acute (biliary) pancreatitis.

stem: 34 year old man presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain for 12 hours Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness serum amylase: 250 IU/dl. Chest X-ray was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Source key A (CT) for confirming the diagnosis when amylase is only mildly raised; other versions of this recall keyed ultrasound. CT confirms pancreatitis when biochemistry is equivocal.

why.D: The other versions' key (for the cause).

stem: Redundant mesentery of which part of the gastrointestinal tract can result in volvulus?
expl: A long redundant sigmoid mesentery with a narrow base lets the sigmoid twist → sigmoid volvulus.

why.B: Gastric volvulus is linked to hiatus hernia/laxity of ligaments.
why.D: Small-bowel volvulus is usually around adhesions/malrotation.

stem: Which one of the following represent 'Charcot's triad in acute cholangitis?

opts.t: Right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting
Right upper quadrant pain with tenderness and fever
Right upper quadrant pain, fever and hypotension
Right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice

expl: Charcot's triad = RUQ pain, fever and jaundice.

stem: A 24- year-old married lady presented to the emergency department complaining of cramping right iliac fossa pain which became generalized all over the abdomen associated with fainting since 6 hours. On examination she was tachycardic and hypotensive with diffuse abdominal tenderness Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Married woman, cramping RIF pain becoming generalized, fainting and tachycardia → haemoperitoneum from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

why.A: Perforated appendicitis doesn't cause fainting/haemorrhagic shock early.
why.B: Meckel's bleeding is painless PR bleeding in children.
why.C: DU perforation starts in the epigastrium.

stem: A 25-year-old male patient presented to the emergency department complaining of right lower quadrant abdominal pain since 5 days associated with nausea and loss of appetite. On examination, he was febrile with tender mass in the right iliac fossa. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in his management?
expl: RLQ pain for 5 days with a tender mass → US (or CT) to distinguish phlegmon from abscess before deciding drainage vs antibiotics.

why.B: Standard appendectomy on a mass is hazardous.

stem: A 33.year-old male patient presented to the emergency department complaining of severe sudden epigastric pain since 4 hours associated with two episodes of vomiting. Abdominal examination revealed a very tender epigastric region. Laboratory values showed WBC: 12.7x 109 /L. serum amylase: 231 IU/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
expl: Sudden severe epigastric pain with tenderness → erect CXR first (perforation).

why.A: Endoscopy is contraindicated if perforation is suspected.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting. Laboratory values showed serum amylase: 1246 IU/L. Which of the following is the appropriate initial step in management of this patient?
expl: Acute pancreatitis (amylase 1246) → the initial step is IV fluid resuscitation (goal-directed crystalloid, Ringer's lactate).

why.B: US comes after resuscitation to find gallstones.

stem: A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, jaundice and fever. On examination he was febrile with a tender right upper quadrant. Laboratory values showed Leukocytosis, and elevated liver function test. Ultrasound revealed dilated intra and extrahepatic biliary tree. Which of the following is the appropriate initial step in management of this patient?
expl: Cholangitis — the first step is resuscitation with IV fluids, then IV antibiotics, then ERCP within 24–48 h.

stem: A 50-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, vomiting and distension and increased bowel sound. Plain abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels, a rounded opacity on the right side and air within the biliary tract. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rigler's triad: small-bowel obstruction + pneumobilia + an ectopic (rounded) gallstone = gallstone ileus.

stem: A 60-year-old male presented with sudden onset abdominal pain, distension and constipation. Abdominal examination reveals a huge asymmetrical abdominal distension. Plain abdominal x-ray shows a hugely distended large bowel which looks like 'omega’. The most likely diagnosis is?
expl: Huge asymmetrical distension with a hugely distended loop rising from the pelvis = sigmoid volvulus.

why.A: Colo-colic intussusception is rare in adults.
why.D: Pseudo-obstruction is symmetrical colonic dilatation in medical patients.

stem: A 35-year old male presents with features of intestinal obstruction. Examination reveals a distended abdomen with a grid-iron scar. Which of the following radiological investigations should initially be requested for this patient?
expl: Suspected intestinal obstruction (previous appendectomy) → initial plain abdominal X-ray (dilated loops, air-fluid levels).

why.C: Barium enema is contraindicated in possible strangulation.

stem: In a patient with adhesive intestinal obstruction, which of the following is an indication for urgent surgical intervention?

opts.t: Symptoms persisting for more than 12 hours
Presence of abdominal tenderness on palpation
History of laparotomy in the past

expl: In adhesive SBO, signs of peritonism (tenderness, guarding), fever, tachycardia, raised WBC/lactate suggest strangulation → urgent surgery.

why.A: 12 h of symptoms alone doesn't mandate surgery (wait 48–72 h).
why.C: Previous laparotomy is the cause, not an indication.
why.D: Green NG aspirate is expected in SBO.

stem: A 75-year-old male in the medical ward with multiple medical problems develops abdominal distension and constipation. Investigations reveal hypokalemia, hypoalbuminemia, distended small and large bowel with multiple airfluid levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Medical patient with hypokalaemia and hypoalbuminaemia, dilated small AND large bowel with air-fluid levels → adynamic (paralytic) ileus.

why.A: Mechanical obstruction has a transition point and a collapsed distal bowel.
why.D: Primary peritonitis gives fever and ascites.

stem: A 35 year old woman presented to the emergency department with a history of sudden severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting. Physical examination revealed tender epigastric area serum amylase was 1534 IU/L. Which of the following is the appropriate initial imaging study for this patient?
expl: Acute pancreatitis (amylase 1534) → abdominal US to look for gallstones.

why.B: CT is for diagnostic doubt or complications after 72 h.

stem: A 42-year old female patient presented to the emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant pain, yellowish discoloration of sclera and dark urine since one week. Which of the following is the appropriate initial investigation for this patient?
expl: Jaundice with RUQ pain → initial US (stones, ductal dilatation).

stem: Which one of the following is a supportive sign of acute appendicitis?

opts.t: Increase of pain with testicular elevation
Referred pain in the right side with pressure on the left side of the abdomen
Relief of pain in lower abdomen with extension of thigh
Relief of pain in lower abdomen with internal rotation of right thigh

expl: Rovsing's sign: pressure in the LIF causes pain in the RIF (gas displaced towards the caecum) — supports appendicitis.

why.A: Pain on testicular elevation isn't appendicitis.
why.C: Psoas sign = pain on hip extension (not relief).
why.D: Obturator sign = pain on internal rotation (not relief).

stem: In a patient with complete proximal jejunal obstruction, which of the following combined signs and symptoms will be more prominent?
expl: High (proximal jejunal) obstruction → early profuse vomiting and pain with little distension; constipation is late.

stem: Which of the following is the commonest cause of small intestinal obstruction in adults?
expl: Adhesions are the commonest cause of SBO in adults (hernias in a virgin abdomen).

stem: Acute appendicitis is diagnosed mainly by which of the following?
expl: Appendicitis is diagnosed mainly clinically (history and examination, Alvarado); imaging confirms in unclear cases.

stem: A 70-year-old diabetic male patient presented to the ER complaining of left lower quadrant abdominal pain and constipation since 2 days. On examination the vital signs, heart rate 72 beats/min, blood pressure 120/80. T 38.5 C with tenderness in the left iliac fossa. White cell count was 14.5*109/ L. CT scan of the abdomen revealed thick wall of sigmoid colon, with no abdominal collection. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
expl: Stable diabetic with LLQ pain, fever and constipation = uncomplicated diverticulitis → IV fluids and IV antibiotics (CT to stage).

why.D: Endoscopy is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis (perforation risk).

stem: A 66-year-old male patient on aspirin for ischemic heart disease presented with sudden sever epigastric pain since 6 hours. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness guarding with resonant percussion over the liver. White blood cell count: 15.3 x 109/mm3, serum amylase: 271 IU/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Aspirin + sudden severe epigastric pain + diffuse guarding + loss of liver dullness (resonance from free air) = perforated peptic ulcer.

stem: A 50-year old male presented with features of sigmoid volvulus which was successfully reduced by colonoscopy What is the further appropriate treatment to prevent recurrence?
expl: After successful endoscopic reduction of sigmoid volvulus, recurrence is ~50–60% → elective sigmoid colectomy (same admission).

why.B: A colostomy isn't the definitive prevention.

stem: An old man presented with right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and fever .. your initial management is:
expl: Cholangitis (pain, jaundice, fever) → first IV fluids (resuscitation), then antibiotics, then ERCP.

stem: An old female took aspirin for joint pain and is presenting with one day history of abdominal pain , Dx is
expl: Elderly woman on aspirin for joint pain with abdominal pain → NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease.

why.B: Colon cancer has a longer history.
why.D: Crohn's is unlikely with this story.

stem: A patient on aspirin presented with abdominal pain and resonant percussion under diaphragm Dx is
expl: On aspirin + abdominal pain + resonance over the liver (free air) → perforated peptic ulcer.

why.D: Volvulus gives distension, not liver resonance.

stem: A married lady presented to ER with RIF abdominal pain and now is becoming severe and diffuse and history of fainting, tachycardia and hypotension , Dx is :
expl: Married woman, RIF pain becoming severe and diffuse, fainting, tachycardia and hypotension → ruptured ectopic pregnancy (haemoperitoneum).

why.B: A ruptured ovarian cyst rarely causes shock.
why.D: Diverticulitis is LIF and older patients.

stem: air in biliary tree:
expl: Air in the biliary tree (pneumobilia) + obstruction = gallstone ileus (cholecystoenteric fistula).

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a right upper quadrant abdominal pain for 36 hours, associated with vomiting. She also complains of pain at the tip of her right shoulder. On examination, she looks to be in moderate pain. She does not look pale or jaundiced. Her vital signs are normal except for a temperature of 38.50 C Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Which of the following would be most helpful in confirming the diagnosis?
expl: RUQ pain with right shoulder-tip referral (biliary) → abdominal US first.

why.C: Gastroscopy is for upper GI mucosa.
why.D: Amylase is a lab test, not imaging; it doesn't confirm biliary disease.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents to your emergency department with acute episodic pain radiating to the back, the patient is febrile 38.8 and his serum amylase is 1854 U/L. Which one of the following is the most important initial imaging modality to confirm the cause?
expl: Fever with back pain and high amylase → abdominal ultrasound is the key initial imaging to find the cause (gallstones/cholecystitis, CBD). The source notes that amylase isn't specific — cholecystitis also fits.

why.A: Excludes perforation, but doesn't find the cause.

stem: 75 year old woman with a history of congestive heart failure presents with diffuse abdominal pain for 2 hours. On examination, she has distended abdomen, diffuse tenderness, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Occult blood test was positive. Labs results are remarkable for high WBCs and Lactic acid. BP: 95/60 mmHg HR: 110/min RR: 22/min Temp: 38.5 C SpO2: 100% on room air What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: CHF + diffuse pain, distension, hyperactive bowel sounds and positive occult blood → mesenteric ischaemia.

stem: Which parts of the gastrointestinal tract will be ischemic in case of thrombosis of the superior mesenteric artery?
expl: The SMA supplies the midgut: small intestine (jejunum, ileum), caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal ⅔ of the transverse colon.

stem: A 70 year old female patient presents with severe acute abdominal pain, her ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Basic labs are as follows: WBC: 24×109, Hb: 12 g/dl, PLT: 150×103, Lactate: 8 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: AF (embolic source), severe pain, leukocytosis and lactate 8 → acute bowel (mesenteric) ischaemia.

why.A: SMA syndrome is duodenal compression after weight loss.
why.C: Torsion doesn't fit AF/lactate 8 in a 70-year-old.
why.D: Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever without such lactate.

stem: A patient presented with acute epigastric pain and high amylase level (case basically suggests acute pancreatitis) upon physical examination there was a dark discoloration on the patient's flanks. What's the name of this clinical sign?
expl: Flank ecchymosis = Grey Turner's sign (retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking to the flanks) in haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Cullen's = periumbilical.

stem: A forty-year-old male taking low dose aspirin is brought to ER with sudden onset of severe epigastric pain. He is a known case of duodenal ulcer. On examination he is tachycardic with pulse of 125/min, normotensive. Examination of his abdomen reveals tenderness and guarding over all quadrants What is the most appropriate investigation?
expl: Sudden severe epigastric pain in a known DU patient on aspirin, with tachycardia and generalized guarding = perforation until proven otherwise → erect chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm.

why.A: Never do endoscopy in suspected perforation (insufflation worsens the leak).
why.B: A barium enema looks at the colon; barium in the peritoneum is dangerous.
why.C: Amylase can rise mildly in perforation; it doesn't confirm it.

stem: A 45-year-old man, who has hypertension and controlled type 2 diabetes, presented 4 days post-exploratory laparotomy for perforated acute appendicitis with grossly distended abdomen and mild generalized discomfort. He has sluggish bowel sounds, vomiting and constipation. His vitals are normal, and his investigations revealed white blood count of 8 (normal range 3.5-10.5) and multiple air-fluid levels in the abdominal X-ray. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Post-laparotomy (peritonitis) distension, vomiting, sluggish bowel sounds, air-fluid levels with normal WBC and vitals on day 4 → paralytic ileus.

why.C: Obstruction gives hyperactive (not sluggish) sounds; early adhesive SBO is less likely.

stem: A 65-year old man presented with abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation for 2 days. He was diagnosed with large bowel obstruction. He never had any abdominal surgery before. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Large-bowel obstruction in a 65-year-old with no surgery → malignancy most likely.

why.D: Hernias usually obstruct the small bowel.

stem: An 80 y/o man known case of ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, and gallstones. Presents with a history of severe abdominal pain and vomiting for one day. On examination he looks sick, in pain, with blood pressure of 105/60. Heart rate of 110 beat/minute and temperature of 38.3 C. His abdomen is mildly rigid with no rebound tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: IHD + AF + severe pain, sick and hypotensive → acute mesenteric ischaemia.

why.A: AAA would give a pulsatile mass/back pain.
why.C: Gallstones suggest pancreatitis, but the embolic source and sickness point to ischaemia.

stem: A 19-year old woman, presents with one-day history of lower abdominal pain that increased over the last 4 hours. She has no history of vomiting or fever. She gave a history of amenorrhea for the last two months. On examination, she looks sick, sweaty with cold skin. Her blood pressure is 90/50. And heart rate of 130 beat/minute. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: 2 months' amenorrhoea + worsening lower abdominal pain without vomiting/fever → ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

why.D: Ovarian cyst rupture doesn't explain the amenorrhoea.

stem: What is the imaging modality when evaluating a suspected bowel perforation?
expl: Suspected perforation → plain X-ray (erect CXR/abdomen) is the first imaging for free air; CT if unclear.

why.A: CT is more sensitive but second-line.
why.D: US isn't used for free air.

stem: A 25 y/o admitted through emergency department complaining of right iliac fossa pain for 5 days. Physical examination revealed tenderness and fullness in right iliac fossa. Ultrasound showed acute appendicitis with significant pus collection in right iliac fossa. Temperature: 38.5 0C, BP; 80/40, Pulse: 115/min. Which of the following is the definitive step in management of this patient?
expl: Resuscitation and antibiotics come first, but the DEFINITIVE treatment of an abscess is drainage (source control).

stem: Which of the following infecting organism carries the risk of upper GI contamination and neoplastic diseases?
expl: H. pylori colonizes the upper GI tract and causes peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

stem: What is a key clinical sign indicating inflammation of the gallbladder?
expl: Murphy's sign — inspiratory arrest on palpation of the RUQ — indicates gallbladder inflammation.

stem: A patient who is a known case of arthritis presents with acute abdominal pain and pneumoperitoneum on imaging. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Arthritis → NSAIDs → peptic ulcer → perforation → pneumoperitoneum.

why.C: Ectopic gives blood, not free air.

stem: What are the causes of extramural obstruction?
expl: Extramural (outside the wall) causes: adhesions, hernia, volvulus. Cancer and Crohn's are mural; a foreign body is intraluminal.

stem: Which artery of the gastrointestinal tract if thrombosed will cause ischemia in Jejunum, ilium & cecum?
expl: Jejunum, ileum and caecum are midgut — supplied by the SMA.

stem: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction
expl: Adhesions and bands are the commonest cause of SBO.

stem: 45 y/o woman had a history of open appendectomy 2 years ago, came to the ER complaining of abdominal pain and distension, there was an X-ray pic, (incomplete) What is the management? Original image from 434 Q56
srcNote: (Principles of Laparoscopic Surgery) there’s adhesions we can’t go laparoscopically
expl: Keyed answer: exploratory laparotomy (source note: "there are adhesions, we can't go laparoscopically"). The full scenario/X-ray wasn't recalled — with signs of strangulation or failed conservative care, adhesive SBO is operated on; a stable patient would first get NG decompression ± Gastrografin.

why.A: Laparoscopy is difficult with dense adhesions (source reasoning).
why.D: Gastrografin is diagnostic/therapeutic in stable adhesive SBO — not keyed here.

stem: A woman presented with severe abdominal pain along with rigidity, guarding and rebound tenderness. Which of the following is the appropriate first imaging modality?
expl: Peritonitis signs (rigidity, guarding, rebound) → upright CXR first for free air.

stem: 18 y/o boy presented to the emergency department with right lower quadrant pain for 18 hours. On examination, there was tenderness on palpation of right lower quadrant with rebound tenderness, otherwise normal. Vital signs were BP: 100/60 mmHg, HR: 80/min, RR: 18/min, Tem: 37.8 C, SpO2: 100% on room air. Which of the following is the best next step?
expl: Young man with RLQ pain 18 h and rebound → CT abdomen/pelvis to confirm appendicitis.

stem: A 35-year-old man came to the emergency department complaining of acute epigastric pain radiating to his back associated with vomiting six times. On abdominal examination he is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, his temperature is 39 C, Serum Amylase is 2500 U/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute epigastric pain radiating to the back with repeated vomiting and epigastric tenderness = acute pancreatitis (confirm with lipase/amylase).

stem: A 48-year-old female was admitted through the emergency department with abdominal pain, abdominal distention, nausea and vomiting for three days. She hasn’t passed gas or stool for 1 day. Her past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidemia and open appendectomy Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
expl: Obstruction after a previous open appendectomy → adhesions/bands are the commonest cause of SBO.

why.C: Possible but less likely with this history.

stem: Recall — sudden epigastric pain, X-ray shown (free gas). What is the diagnosis?
ansText: Perforated viscus — free air under the diaphragm on the erect film.

stem: 58 Year Old Male came to hospital with obstructive symptoms, CT showed Rectosigmoid obstruction and secondary liver and lung deposit. What would you do?

opts.t: Nothing as there is secondary deposit

expl: Obstructing rectosigmoid cancer with liver and lung metastases → palliate the obstruction with a defunctioning (transverse) colostomy.

why.C: Bypass is less practical for a rectosigmoid tumor.
why.D: The obstruction must be relieved regardless of metastases.

stem: History of a patient with nausea and vomiting with acute abdominal pain. X-ray shown below. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute pain with the classic X-ray of a hugely dilated inverted-U loop = sigmoid volvulus.

why.C: Too vague — the X-ray is specific.
why.D: Intussusception gives a target sign on US/CT.

stem: A 51 y\o man who underwent abdomino-perineal resection for 5 days ago. Was complaining of chest pain and dyspnea. Physical examination normal. CBC and cardiac enzymes normal Temperature 37.2 Blood pressure 85\50 mmHg Pulse 120 beat\min Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic investigations?
expl: Post-operative (APR, pelvic surgery) patient with sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, hypotension and tachycardia, normal cardiac enzymes → pulmonary embolism → CT pulmonary angiography.

why.B: Echo shows RV strain but doesn't confirm PE.
why.D: CXR is usually normal in PE.

stem: 35 y\o patient came to ER complaining of epigastric pain for 4 days. Physical examination reveals epigastric tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory values showed normal amylase and High WBC. He underwent exploratory laparotomy and found to have duodenal ulcer with diffuse peritoneal soiling with purulent material. Temperature : 39 Blood pressure: 85\50 mmHg. Pulse: 125 beat\min Which of the following characterize the shock state of this patient?
srcNote: (Acute abdomen). septic shock, Infection triggers a cytokine-mediated proinflammatory response that results in peripheral vasodilation, redistribution of blood flow, endothelial cell activation, increased vascular permeability and the formation of microthrombi within the microcirculation. Cardiac output typically increases in septic shock to compensate for the peripheral vasodilation. However, despite a global increase in oxygen delivery, microcirculatory dysfunction impairs oxygen delivery to the cells. Compounding disturbances in oxygen delivery, mitochondrial dysfunction blocks the normal bioenergetic pathways within the cell impairing oxygen utilization. Davidson page number 18, chapter one Year 427
expl: Purulent peritonitis → septic (distributive) shock → cytokine-driven peripheral vasodilation (warm shock), increased permeability.

why.C: Septic shock can be hyperdynamic, but its defining feature is vasodilation (the key).

stem: A known afib patient presents to the ER with an acute abdomen. CT scan revealed pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the diagnosis?
expl: AF + acute abdomen + pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall) = advanced bowel ischaemia.

stem: A 24 year old lady presents to the ER with a sudden severe RLQ abdominal pain that started yesterday. Which of the following tests is important to help you reach the diagnosis?
expl: Any woman of childbearing age with acute lower/RLQ pain → pregnancy test first (ectopic).

stem: A female patient presents to the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the right shoulder. The pain began yesterday. She has been on Monjaro injections for weight loss for the past 3 months. On examination, she is febrile, hypotensive with a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and reports passing dark, tea-colored urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: No answer key provided in the source.
expl: The source had no key. Rapid weight loss (Mounjaro) → gallstones; RUQ pain + fever + dark (tea-coloured) urine = jaundice → Charcot's triad, with hypotension → acute (severe) cholangitis.

why.A: Cholecystitis doesn't cause jaundice/dark urine or shock usually.
why.B: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back.
why.C: A liver abscess gives fever and RUQ pain but rarely obstructive jaundice.

stem: A 56-year-old man is in the ICU after major abdominal trauma and massive fluid resuscitation. He is hemodynamically stable but develops progressive abdominal distension, decreased urine output, and increasing ventilatory pressures. Measurement of intra-abdominal pressure shows a value of 32 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, rising airway pressures) = abdominal compartment syndrome (32 mmHg here, after massive resuscitation).

why.B: Possible cause, but the diagnosis is ACS.

stem: A patient who uses NSAIDs came with a perforated ulcer. What to do?
expl: A perforated peptic ulcer is closed with an omental (Graham) patch — open or laparoscopic — plus washout; then stop NSAIDs, PPI, and treat H. pylori.

why.C: Roux-en-Y is a bypass/reconstruction, not emergency ulcer repair.
why.D: Nissen fundoplication is for GERD/hiatus hernia.

stem: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
expl: Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide (alcohol second).

stem: A patient diagnosed with pancreatitis a few weeks ago is now found to have a pseudocyst. Which condition indicates the need for surgical intervention?
expl: Source key A. A pseudocyst causing gastric/duodenal outlet obstruction is an indication for intervention (surgical/endoscopic drainage). Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm is treated by angio-embolisation; splenic vein thrombosis doesn't by itself need surgery.

why.D: Also an indication, but obstruction was keyed.

stem: 19 y/o present to the ER with perforated appendicitis and we did laparoscopic appendectomy with multiple time wash the abdomen we discharge the patient and he present later with persistent fever with RLQ tenderness without sign of peritonitis HR and blood pressure is normal WBC is 14 after doing CT we found 6 CM RLQ collection what is the best management?
expl: A stable patient with a 6 cm well-defined abscess → antibiotics + image-guided percutaneous drainage (less invasive than surgery).

why.A: Surgery is for failed percutaneous drainage or peritonitis.
why.D: Antibiotics alone don't drain a large collection.

stem: Pregnant lady came with RUQ/RLQ pain (not sure), what is the initial test to do?
expl: In pregnancy, ultrasound is the first imaging (no radiation); MRI if non-diagnostic; CT only if necessary.

stem: patient presented with strangulated hernia. Where do you expect to find it
expl: A hernia obstructs the bowel from outside the wall → extramural (extrinsic) cause.

stem: case about distended abdomen post Cholecystectomy. X-ray showed stone in the small bowel. Diagnosis:-
expl: Distension with a stone seen in the small bowel = gallstone ileus. (The recall said "post-cholecystectomy", which is unusual — classically the gallbladder is still present and has fistulated.)

stem: case about perforated diverticulitis “ history of diverticulitis and IV ABx with air under diaphragm on CxR” what is the next step in management
expl: Diverticulitis with free air under the diaphragm = perforation with generalized peritonitis → laparotomy (usually Hartmann's procedure).

why.A: Free perforation needs surgery, not antibiotics alone.
why.C: Hartmann's is the likely procedure done at laparotomy, but the keyed next step is laparotomy.

stem: pregnant women in 24 week gestation presented with abdominal pain and vomiting cleared from oby-gyn, in the physical pain in right side , what is best imaging modality for diagnosis appendicitis
expl: At 24 weeks, if US can't see the appendix, MRI (no radiation, no contrast) is the best imaging to diagnose appendicitis.

why.A: US is first but often non-diagnostic later in pregnancy.
why.C: CT exposes the fetus — only if MRI unavailable.

stem: 89 year old patient presents with 3 day history of inability to pass flatus, she previously had 5 months constipation imaging revealed obstruction in sigmoid colon with no distended small bowel. She has multiple liver and lung metastases. What is the management
expl: Source key: colectomy — a palliative resection of the obstructing sigmoid tumor relieves the obstruction and prevents bleeding/perforation; many would also accept a stent or colostomy in an 89-year-old with metastases. Follow the source key for the exam.

why.C: A defunctioning colostomy is a reasonable alternative.
why.D: A stent is another palliative option, especially in frail patients.

stem: After surgery, you notice your patient having abdominal bloating and abdominal distension, the x-ray shows an air–fluid level. What are you going to do next?

opts.t: keep patient Npo, and nasogastric decompression
Do CT to confirm the diagnosis

expl: Post-op distension with air-fluid levels (ileus or early obstruction) → conservative: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, correct electrolytes.

why.C: CT only if not settling or signs of strangulation.

stem: A 24-year-old female presented to the emergency room with periumbilical pain associated with Nausea and vomiting. Her pain then became in the RLQ. B-HCG was normal. What’s the best initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Keyed: young woman with classic migration and negative β-hCG → US first (no radiation; also assesses ovaries). CT if US is inconclusive.

why.A: CT is the adult standard per the doctor, but the key chose US in a young woman.

stem: 60 y o female with a history of multiple emergency visits, come to ER with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had a history of cholecystectomy 30 years ago. She had a history of alcohol intake for a long time. High amylase and lipase with normal bilirubin.What is the diagnosis?
expl: Long-standing alcohol, previous cholecystectomy (gallstones unlikely) and normal bilirubin → alcoholic pancreatitis.

stem: A female patient on NSAIDS for arthritis(or some surgery a while back, I can’t remember :)) presented to the ER with epigastric pain that started 8 hours ago, and shifted to the right iliac fossa. On examination, the patient had generalized tenderness specifically on the epigastric and right iliac fossa. With guarding and rigidity, What's the best management?

opts.t: Observe and CT abdomen after 48 hours

expl: NSAID user with epigastric pain that shifted to the RIF and generalized guarding/rigidity → perforated ulcer with peritonitis (gastric contents tracking down the right gutter — mimics appendicitis) → exploratory laparotomy.

why.B: Observing peritonitis for 48 h is dangerous.

stem: A pregnant lady presenting in the second trimester with acute right sided abdominal pain, she has not had any vomiting in the first trimester and now presents with episodes of vomiting. What is the most common non-obstetrics surgical cause of the pain?
expl: Appendicitis is the most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy (~1 in 1500), then cholecystitis.

stem: Patient presented with cholecystitis and fever, but with no jaundice. The US shows thickened walls of the gallbladder but no stone in the CBD. What is the management?
expl: The source had no key. Acute calculous cholecystitis without jaundice or CBD stones → laparoscopic cholecystectomy (early, same admission). ERCP/MRCP are only needed if CBD stones are suspected.

why.B: ERCP is unnecessary with no CBD stone.
why.D: MRCP is unnecessary — no jaundice, normal CBD.

stem: A case of a chron’s patient who underwent hemicolectomy as a management for his symptoms. However, he presented a few days later post-op complaining of signs and symptoms of local peritonitis. What’s the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms ?
expl: Local peritonitis a few days after a bowel resection with anastomosis → anastomotic leak until proven otherwise.

why.B: Causes recurrence later, not acute peritonitis.

stem: A 32 year old man presented with ruptured appendicitis. A Laparoscopic procedure was done. 4 days post-op, he had a fever and and a right lower quadrant pain, but the wound looked OK with no redness or discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever and RLQ pain on day 4 after appendectomy for a ruptured appendix with a normal wound = intra-abdominal (pelvic/RLQ) abscess — an organ-space SSI.

why.A: Cecal perforation/leak would give peritonitis and sepsis.

stem: A 76 years old woman was admitted to the ICU due to pneumonia. She was given 3 vasopressors and the appropriate management. In Spite of that, her BP was 86/45, and HR was 112. 4 days after the admission to the ICU she became anuric. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: An ICU patient on high-dose vasopressors with persistent low flow is at risk of non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (splanchnic vasoconstriction). The source key is B.

stem: A 45 year old female was admitted as a diagnosis of acute cholecystitis. Which of the following symptoms is associated with charcot's triad in diagnosis of acute cholangitis?
expl: Source key B. Charcot's triad is fever, RUQ pain and jaundice; of the options, pruritus is the one that accompanies cholestatic jaundice.

stem: A 60 y/o man presented with abdominal pain that started 2 hours ago, followed by nausea and vomiting of bilious material. He has no chest pain, no history of cardiac problems, and the ECG was normal. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute abdominal pain followed by bilious vomiting, with cardiac causes excluded → small-bowel obstruction (bile means the block is distal to the ampulla).

why.C: LBO presents with distension and constipation, vomiting late.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding Nasogastric tube?

opts.t: Not usually contraindicated in skull base fractures
Insert the tube superiorly into the nose

expl: Placement is confirmed by aspirating gastric contents (pH <5.5) ± X-ray. NG tubes are contraindicated in skull-base fractures, are a clean (not sterile) procedure, and are passed backwards along the nasal floor, not upwards.

stem: What is the most efficient non-invasive investigation for Small bowel obstruction?
expl: Plain abdominal X-ray is the quickest, cheapest non-invasive test for SBO (dilated loops, air-fluid levels).

why.D: US is less reliable for obstruction.

stem: Appendicular artery arises from which of the following barnches?
expl: The appendicular artery is a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the SMA), running in the mesoappendix.

stem: Patient presented with cholecytsitis complicated by choledolithaisis. What is the management?
expl: Cholecystitis with CBD stones → clear the CBD with ERCP and remove the gallbladder (same admission).

stem: Patient is presented with abdominal pain and mild distension , abdominal examination shows multiple scars from previous surgeries , rectal exam show empty rectal vault

opts.t: CT abdomen with oral and IV contrast

expl: Suspected adhesive obstruction (multiple scars, empty rectum, distension) → CT abdomen with oral and IV contrast to confirm, find the transition point and look for strangulation.

stem: Which one is an indication for surgery in small bowel obstruction?
expl: SBO in a virgin abdomen (no adhesions) has a different cause (hernia, tumour, band) → surgery is indicated rather than conservative treatment.

why.A: Vomiting is treated with NG decompression.
why.C: Electrolytes are corrected; they aren't an indication.

stem: A 65-year-old male presented to the emergency room with a picture of bowel obstruction. A CT scan of the abdomen showed an ultra low rectal mass with bi-lobar liver metastasis, lung metastasis as well as retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Which or the following is the best management option for his current condition?
expl: Obstruction from an ultra-low rectal mass with widespread metastases → palliate the obstruction with a diverting stoma. Ultra-low tumors are not suitable for stents (tenesmus, pain, migration).

why.C: Stents are poor for ultra-low rectal tumors.

stem: 50 year old patient post Roux-e-Y procedure after 4 years he came with severe colics in the center of the abdomen he was hemodynamically stable and all his vitals were alright. Which of the following is most commonly the cause of his presentation?
expl: Source key: adhesions (commonest cause of SBO after any abdominal surgery). After Roux-en-Y, internal hernia is the classic special concern for intermittent colicky pain.

why.D: Marginal ulcer causes epigastric pain, not colic.

stem: A 20 years old medical student who is a smoker presents to the ER with severe epigastric, which of the following should be done to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Severe epigastric pain in a young smoker (suspected peptic ulcer) → upper GI endoscopy confirms it (after excluding perforation).

why.C: H. pylori testing doesn't show the ulcer.
why.D: Breath test doesn't show the ulcer.

stem: Which of the following is most likely to be done during a nasogastric intubation?

opts.t: The tube is initially inserted superiorly into the nose
Auscultation is done to confirm the proper placement of the tube

expl: Source key B — classic bedside check: insufflate air and auscultate over the epigastrium (aspiration with pH testing and X-ray are more reliable). The tube is passed backwards along the nasal floor, not upwards.

stem: Nurse in the surgery ward called the surgical team to induce a Nasogastric tube. Why do you think ?

opts.t: For patient who has elective cholecystectomy

expl: NG tubes are inserted for GI bleeding (to assess/lavage), decompression (obstruction, ileus) and feeding. Not routine for elective cholecystectomy; contraindicated in nasal fracture.

why.B: The other year's key considered this an indication too.

stem: Patient presented to ER with abdominal pain, and you have been called to insert NGT, Which one of the following is an indication for NGT?
expl: Source key A: in a perforated duodenal ulcer an NG tube decompresses the stomach and reduces peritoneal contamination. NGT is contraindicated in basal skull and maxillofacial fractures; it isn't needed for elective lap chole.

stem: Patient 24 years old was presented to an emergency with sudden severe abdominal pain in the upper quadrant for 6 hours. What's the next step in management?
srcNote: Drs told us the answer. You have to exclude perforation.
expl: Sudden severe upper abdominal pain → erect CXR for free air first.

stem: Patient presented through the emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain with jaundice yellow discoloration of sclera and dark urine and vomiting for 6 days and fever temperature (39.6) and US revealing intrahepatic and extrahepatic dilatation of biliary tree what is the most effective initial treatment?
srcNote: Ascending cholangitis, The pt has been vomiting for 6 days so we should replace fluids first. Year 435
expl: Six days of vomiting + sepsis (cholangitis) → first restore volume with IV fluids, then antibiotics and ERCP.

why.A: Essential too, but fluid resuscitation first in a dehydrated septic patient.

stem: A 28-year-old man presented with a history of reducible right inguinal hernia for 2 years which became painful since 16 hours associated with progressive abdominal distention and vomiting. Physical examination revealed distended abdomen, exaggerated bowel sound, tender right inguinal swelling with red discoloration of the overlying skin. Blood pressure 110/65 mmHg Heart rate 85 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 18/min. Test Result Normal value WBC 9.8 4-10.5 x 10 9 L. Erect abdominal X-ray: Multiple air-fluid levels. Which of the following is the most likely hernia complication?
expl: A known reducible hernia that becomes painful with distension and vomiting (obstruction) and is now tense and tender → strangulated (the most advanced, surgical emergency).

why.B: Obstructed is possible, but painful tense hernia with systemic signs = strangulation (keyed).

stem: 22 years old pregnant woman for 7 month complaining of right flank pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Right flank pain in late pregnancy: the appendix is pushed up toward the flank, and pyelonephritis (hydronephrosis of pregnancy, right side) is common → both must be considered.

why.B: Diverticulitis is left-sided and older patients.

stem: A 70-year-old lady presented to the hospital with a history of passing bright red blood mixed with stool for 2 weeks. Review of symptoms reveals low appetite, constipation and an approximately 4 kg weight loss over the last 2 months. She denies any history of any abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting or fever, but she feels lethargic. On examination she is pale. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for her presentation?
expl: Elderly with blood mixed with stool, constipation, poor appetite and weight loss → colon cancer.

why.A: IBD in a 70-year-old with weight loss is less likely.
why.B: Ischaemic colitis gives sudden pain + bloody diarrhoea.
why.D: Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever.

stem: 45 years old women came complaining of abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension with hyperactive bowel sounds and vitals are normal?
srcNote: , (Intestinal obstruction) this case most likely to be small bowel obstruction and once suspected the most immediate thing to do is to give IV infusion to preserve hydration. Davidson 6th e p245
expl: Suspected small bowel obstruction with normal vitals → start IV fluids (NPO, NG tube) before imaging.

stem: What is the most specific and sensitive imaging modality to diagnose acute cholecystitis ?
expl: Source key C — ultrasound is the first-line and most practical test. (Strictly, HIDA scan is the most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis.)

why.B: Actually the most sensitive/specific, but not keyed.

stem: A 51 years old male underwent exploratory laparotomy 3 weeks ago. Patient presented to the ER with right epigastric pain for 2 weeks. Patient was febrile (38.8) and with high WBCs (18,000) CT abdomen showed large intra-abdominal collection (12*18 cm ) what is the most appropriate next step ?
expl: A large intra-abdominal collection after laparotomy → image-guided percutaneous drainage first (compilers marked "not sure").

why.D: Reserved for failed drainage or peritonitis.

stem: 24 years old married female came with severe abdominal pain with missed menstrual cycle for 2 months, vitals were high blood pressure 101/94, high heart rate, what is the best next step?
expl: Woman of childbearing age with severe pain and a missed period → β-hCG first (ectopic until proven otherwise).

why.C: Laparotomy if unstable with a positive test.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the ER with a history of 6 episodes of passing large amount of fresh blood per-rectum for 12 hours, but no abdominal pain. On examination, he was pale, with BP of 90/55 mmHg, and HR= 105 b/m, Hemodynamic resuscitation and monitoring was initiated. Nasogastric tube was draining greenish fluids. Which of the following is the most likely source of the bleeding:
expl: Keyed: elderly, large painless fresh rectal bleeding, shocked → angiodysplasia (common in the elderly; diverticulosis is the other main cause).

why.C: UC gives bloody diarrhoea with pain.

stem: In a patient with variceal bleeding after the initial maintenance of airway, breathing and circulation. Which one of the following intravenous medication has been to shown to reduce the mortality?
expl: Antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) in variceal bleeding reduces infections, rebleeding and mortality.

why.A: Erythromycin improves endoscopic view, not survival.
why.D: Octreotide controls bleeding; antibiotics are the mortality-proven drug.

stem: A young male patient who is known to have liver cirrhosis and esophageal varices presented with a complaint of vomiting blood. Fluid resuscitation was initiated. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this patient?
expl: Acute variceal bleeding → after resuscitation start a vasoactive drug (octreotide) + antibiotics, then endoscopic band ligation.

stem: Similar image with a scenario “fever and shortness of breath” What is the diagnosis?
expl: The X-ray shows free subdiaphragmatic air → perforated viscus.

why.D: PUD is the cause of many perforations, but the image diagnosis is perforated viscus.

stem: What is the most useful imaging modality to localize the site of bleeding in a patient with active lower GI bleed?
expl: Active lower GI bleeding → CT angiography localizes the bleeding point (≥ 0.3–0.5 mL/min) and guides embolization.

why.A: Colonoscopy is hard during massive bleeding.
why.D: Double-contrast CT is not for active bleeding.

stem: 70 years old woman complains of several hours of painless massive rectal bleeding. Nasogastric aspirate shows bile but no blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Painless massive rectal bleeding in an elderly patient with an NG aspirate containing bile and no blood (upper source excluded) → diverticular bleeding.

why.A: Infective colitis gives diarrhoea and pain.
why.C: Ischaemic colitis gives pain then bloody diarrhoea.

stem: Abdominal pain due to acute appendicitis is felt initially in the periumblical region because the appendix originates embryologically from which of the following?
srcNote: ( Acute Abdomen ) Foregut is felt in epigastric area Midgut is felt around the umbilicus Hindgut is felt in hypogastric/suprapubic area
expl: The appendix is a midgut derivative (SMA, T10) → early visceral pain is felt periumbilically.

stem: While you are doing a surgical rotation, you are asked to palpate the abdomen of a young male admitted with acute appendicitis. When you palpated the left iliac fossa the patient complained of pain in the right iliac fossa. What is the name of this clinical sign?
expl: Palpating the LIF causes RIF pain → Rovsing's sign.

why.B: Obturator = pain on internal rotation of the hip.

stem: In which of the following patients would performance of diagnostic peritoneal lavage is considered an absolute contraindication?

opts.t: Pregnant with hypotension after a blunt trauma
Expanding abdomen after a chest stab wound
Hypotension after car accident with previous abdominal surgery

srcNote: (Acute abdomen) (according to different sources, the only absolute contraindication to diagnostic peritoneal lavage is presence of the need to do exploratory laparotomy)
expl: The only absolute contraindication to DPL is an existing indication for laparotomy — an expanding abdomen after a stab wound needs the OR. Pregnancy and previous surgery are relative contraindications.

stem: A 70 year old male, diabetic, hypertensive and heavy smoker presented last week with hematemesis and was sent for urgent endoscopy. Endoscopy revealed peptic ulcer as the source of bleeding. Today he is back to the emergency with coffee ground vomiting Which of the following endoscopic finding suggests high risk of re-bleeding in this patient? *

opts.t: Presence of scar tissue around the ulcer

expl: Endoscopic stigmata of rebleeding: active bleeding > visible vessel > adherent clot > flat spot > clean base. Of the options, an adherent clot predicts rebleeding.

why.B: A clean flat ulcer is low risk.

stem: A 20 year old male is brought to the hospital with history of vomiting of bright red blood. Upon taking history, the patient admits to drinking alcohol last night and started vomiting later on.
