The initial vomitus was clear, after a few episodes of vomiting he noticed bright red streaks of blood in his vomitus. Which one of the following is most consistent with his presentation?
expl: Clear vomitus followed by bright red blood after binge drinking → Mallory–Weiss tear (mucosal tear at the GEJ from retching).

why.A: Boerhaave gives severe chest pain and sepsis.

stem: A 60 y/o female patient, who is known to have ischemic heart disease and diabetes mellitus presents with acute abdomen pain. Her ECG shows arterial fibrillation. An initial impression of acute abdomen is made and patient admitted for further investigations. Which of the following is most likely to reveal her underlying diagnosis?
expl: Keyed: elderly with IHD, DM and AF + acute abdomen → CT (CT angiography) for mesenteric ischaemia and other causes.

why.B: US can't assess mesenteric vessels well.
why.C: Dipstick doesn't assess an acute abdomen.

stem: A 34 y/o female, who is admitted to the floor 30 minutes ago with acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain. What is the initial investigation you will order for this patient?
expl: Keyed answer: the initial (first) investigation is a CBC (leukocytosis); imaging (US) follows.

why.B: US is the first imaging test.
why.D: LFTs are sent with the CBC, but the key is CBC.

stem: A 40 y/o man presented with acute abdominal pain. The triage nurse told you that his oxygen saturation was 97% on air room, pulse 110/min, BP: 80/60 mmHg. When you examined his abdomen there was a pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. Which one of the following is the initial step of management of this patient?
expl: Hypotension + pulsatile epigastric mass = ruptured AAA → immediate laparotomy (permissive hypotension, no CT in an unstable patient).

why.A: Blood is given en route; it isn't the definitive step.

stem: A 24 y/o married female presented with lower abdominal pain for 6 hours. The initial observation reveal a BP: 90/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min and oxygen saturation of 95% on air room. Which of the following differential diagnoses should be ruled out in this patient?
expl: Lower abdominal pain + shock in a married young woman → the life-threatening diagnosis to exclude is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

stem: A 44 y/o female patient who is known to have gallstones, presents right upper quadrant pain with vomiting and fever. Which clinical sign likely to be positive in this patient?
expl: Gallstones + RUQ pain + fever = acute cholecystitis → Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation).

stem: Which of the following patients will most likely need parenteral nutritional support after surgery?

opts.t: Massive small bowel resection for mesenteric ischemia.
Omental patch closure of perforated duodenal ulcer.
Right hemicolectomy of carcinoma of the caecum.

expl: Massive small-bowel resection (short-bowel syndrome) → parenteral nutrition is needed; the other operations allow early enteral feeding.

stem: An elderly male patient presented with asymmetrical abdominal distension and constipation with tenderness on examination, x-ray showed omega sign, what is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly with asymmetrical distension, constipation and the X-ray "omega" (bent inner tube/coffee bean) sign → sigmoid volvulus.

why.D: Crohn's doesn't produce the omega sign.

stem: A 70 year/old diabetic male, presented with LLQ abdominal tenderness, fever and elevated WBC count, CT abdomen showed thickening of sigmoid wall with no abdominal fluid collection, what is your next step for management:
expl: Keyed: elderly diabetic with uncomplicated diverticulitis (thick wall, no collection) → start with IV fluid resuscitation, then IV antibiotics.

why.B: Antibiotics are given too — the key chose fluids as the first step.

stem: 35 y/o, 6 times bloody, fever, leukocytosis, generalized abdominal tenderness, next step in management is:
expl: Keyed: severe/fulminant colitis (6 bloody stools, fever, leukocytosis) with generalized tenderness (peritonism — possible perforation/toxic colitis) → emergency colectomy. Without peritonism, IV steroids would come first.

why.B: First-line for acute severe UC without peritonitis.
why.C: Colonoscopy risks perforation in severe colitis.

stem: 55 Y/O male presented to have sigmoid volvulus what is the Tx of choice:

opts.t: Admission with IV fluid and resuscitation

expl: Keyed sigmoidopexy (older recall). Current practice: resuscitate → endoscopic detorsion → elective sigmoid colectomy; sigmoidopexy has high recurrence, so resection is the definitive operation (not offered here).

why.B: Resuscitation is the first step, not the treatment of choice.
why.C: "Endoscopic excision" is not a procedure for volvulus.

stem: 24 Y/O married lady, presented with sudden RLQ colicky pain for 6 hours, associated with nausea, fainting, and abdominal tenderness. She is tachycardic and hypotensive. what is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Young married woman, sudden RLQ colicky pain, fainting, tachycardia and hypotension → ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

why.B: Perforated appendicitis doesn't cause early fainting.
why.D: Ischaemia is in the elderly with AF.

stem: most common cause of intestinal obstruction in adults:
expl: Adhesions are the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in adults.

stem: What is the best indicator for appendicitis:

opts.t: Pain in the right iliac fossa when applying pressure in the left side

expl: Keyed: RIF pain when pressing on the left side (Rovsing's) — a specific sign of appendicitis.

why.C: RLQ pain and tenderness alone are less specific.

stem: A 10 years old child presented with RLQ pain, fever, tenderness and guarding ,, with elevated WBC,, what is the next step in management?

opts.t: Give the patient fluids and monitor

expl: A child with clinically obvious appendicitis (RLQ pain, fever, guarding, high WBC) → urgent appendectomy.

why.C: Antibiotics alone aren't standard for clear appendicitis with guarding.

stem: A 2 days, full term, newly born baby, presented with inability to pass meconium, vomiting, distension, what is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A full-term newborn who fails to pass meconium in 48 h, with vomiting and distension → Hirschsprung's disease (aganglionic segment).

why.B: Prune-belly is an abdominal wall defect.
why.C: Pyloric stenosis presents at 3–6 weeks with non-bilious vomiting.

stem: Charcot’s triad:
expl: Charcot's triad = RUQ pain, fever (rigors), jaundice.

why.D: Pain, jaundice and pale stool = obstruction without infection.

stem: air in biliary tree:
expl: Air in the biliary tree = pneumobilia (after sphincterotomy, biliary-enteric anastomosis, or a gallstone fistula — gallstone ileus).

stem: Typical case of appendicitis and with examination there was a mass in LRQ what is the next step:
expl: Keyed appendectomy. Note: a well-formed appendiceal mass (phlegmon) is usually treated conservatively and an abscess drained; the recall says "typical appendicitis", so the key chose surgery.

why.D: Antibiotics are the conservative option for a phlegmon.

stem: Acalculous cholecystitis

opts.t: CT scan is the investigation of choice
Happen usually to ill pt because of another condition
Accounts for 5-10% of the cholecystitis (it is written in Loran’s 20%)

expl: Incomplete stem — it asks for the incorrect statement. Acalculous cholecystitis happens in critically ill patients (burns, ICU, sepsis), makes up 5–10% of cholecystitis and has an aggressive course (gangrene, perforation). US (± HIDA) — not CT — is first-line.

stem: 60 y women has irreducible swelling below and lateral pubic tubercle with nausea and vomiting most likely it is:
expl: An irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle = femoral hernia; with nausea and vomiting → incarcerated and obstructed (femoral hernias strangulate easily).

why.B: Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the tubercle.
why.D: A lymph node doesn't cause vomiting.

stem: Strangulation

opts.t: Is ischemia to the protruded organs

expl: Strangulation = compromised blood supply → ischaemia of the hernia contents. It can be repaired laparoscopically in experienced hands.

stem: 42-year-old female came to the ER with sudden severe epigastric pain that lasts four hours with two episodes of vomiting. The patient had epigastric tenderness, leukocytosis and amylase was 235 what is the initial investigation?
expl: Sudden epigastric pain with tenderness and amylase only mildly raised (235) → erect X-ray first (perforated ulcer can raise amylase).

why.A: Endoscopy is contraindicated if perforation is possible.

stem: Patient with right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice. The right upper quadrant was tender. Ultrasound reveals dilatation of intra- hepatic and extra-hepatic systems. Patient has leukocytosis and elevated LFT. What is the initial treatment?
expl: Cholangitis (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, dilated ducts) → initial management is IV fluids, then antibiotics, then urgent ERCP.

why.B: CT is unnecessary — US already shows dilated ducts.

stem: A 25 y/o male with no history of pervious surgeries, presented to ER with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, on examination: abdomen was distended. X- ray showed multiple air-fluid levels, what is the most appropriate initial management?
expl: SBO (air-fluid levels) in a young man with no previous surgery → first examine the groins (hernia).

why.C: Laparotomy after finding the cause and resuscitating.

stem: Male patient known case of cardiomyopathy presented with central abdominal pain, vomiting passes stool once. On examination: the abdomen was soft, lax with no tenderness and mild exaggerated bowel sounds. Lab result revealed WBC: 26. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Cardiomyopathy + central pain, vomiting, one stool, soft non-tender abdomen (pain out of proportion), high WBC → acute mesenteric vascular occlusion.

stem: Patient with gallstones presented to ER after 4 days complaining of RUQ pain, febrile, US of the gall bladder showed thickened wall with pericystic fluid, what is the best initial management?
expl: Keyed: the best INITIAL management of acute cholecystitis is non-interventional — NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics — before surgery. (The doctor then favours early cholecystectomy in the same admission.)

stem: Patient with abdominal pain, vomiting, and absolute constipation, abdomen X- ray showed (coffee been shaped) pointing to the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Coffee-bean loop pointing to the RUQ with obstruction = sigmoid volvulus (the twisted sigmoid loop rises from the pelvis toward the RUQ).

why.A: Closed loop describes the mechanism; the diagnosis is sigmoid volvulus.

stem: Patient presented with intestinal obstruction symptoms and multiple air fluid level in abdominal x-ray. Right inguinal mass becomes more painful and red. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis of this patient?
expl: Obstruction + an inguinal mass becoming more painful and red (skin changes) = strangulated hernia.

stem: Patient presented with sever epigastric pain that started 5 days ago, on EX: there was epigastric tenderness, the bowl sounds were sluggish and chest Xray shows pleural effusion, amylase 150, what is the best initial management?
expl: Keyed: pain for 5 days — serum amylase falls back within 3–5 days (here 150), but urinary amylase stays raised longer → helps diagnose late-presenting pancreatitis. (Lipase also stays raised longer; CT is the alternative.)

why.B: CT is an alternative but not keyed.
why.C: US looks for gallstones, not the diagnosis.

stem: Patient has severe epigastric abdominal pain for 12 hours with tenderness in examination, chest X-ray was normal, amylase level was 210 (normal is up to 110) what is the appropriate investigations to reach the dx:
expl: Keyed: epigastric pain 12 h, normal CXR, amylase about twice normal → abdominal US (gallstones, biliary cause).

why.B: Urine amylase is for late presentations.

stem: Scenario of female presented with right iliac fossa pain that become generalized all over the abdomen. In examination the heart rate was more than 120 and there was generalized distention and tenderness of the abdomen, what's the next step?
expl: RIF pain that became generalized with tachycardia > 120 and generalized distension/tenderness (peritonitis) → resuscitate first with IV fluids, then laparotomy.
